speechtext: You're reading it through Liberal eyes.
We don't wear blinkers.

In fact, the situation exists and this Bill goes nowhere toward solving those problems.
In conclusion, the people in southwestern Ontario who have had to deal with this chaotic air system at Pearson want action, and they want action in the form of a Bill that will assure them that it will again be safe to fly in the skies.

I would like to echo the point which has been put so forcefully by the Hon. Member for Haldi-mand-Norfolk (Mr. Speller). Certainly, people from southwestern Ontario, and people from the parts of our province who have to travel through Pearson Airport, have faced dangers over and above what people should have to face in using air travel today. We are not talking about some type of pioneering mode of transportation. We are talking about a mode of transportation which a Government has a responsibility to see is operated safely.
Anyone who has followed the recent course of events at Pearson, the long delays which have taken place, the cancellations, the near misses, knows that all of them can be traced back to the false economies that the Government made in not taking on more air traffic controllers to do the job that is necessary with respect to safety. For our constituents, this has represented what they see as a complete dereliction of duty on the part of the Government.
Would the Hon. Member agree with this perception of complete absence of serious concern which should have been there as soon as the decisions were taken to start down the road toward deregulation? If the Hon. Member does agree with that, does he also feel that those Ministers who took the first steps toward deregulation should also have taken the first steps to see to it that air traffic safety was put fully into the equation right from the beginning?
Transportation Accident Investigation Act

I thank the Hon. Member for his comments. He will be aware that we on this side did take those first steps. When the Hon. Member asks whether or not I feel there have been concerns expressed, I believe there have been many concerns expressed. Unfortunately, the action has not been there to follow those concerns.
The Ministers rise daily and state that they are concerned about the situation at Pearson and are concerned about air safety in Canada. In fact, there does not seem to be the actions there to follow through on those concerns.

I would like to thank my colleague for an excellent analysis of the Bill. I am happy to see that the Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport (Mr. Belsher) was present to enjoy it. I am sure he will pass on the comments of the Hon. Member to the Minister to ensure that they are fully understood.
There were two or three points raised indirectly in the speech of my colleague. I would like to go back and discuss them a second time because they are important points.
First, I wish to address the size of the five member board. My suspicion is that for a multimodal board, if that is the route that the Government wishes to go and on which we do not agree, five members is a very small number. How will the Board approach situations? Can that Board handle such situations where, unfortunately, there may be two or three accidents at a time which are quite widely dispersed throughout the country? Will five members have the expertise, the time, and the experience available to relate to these problems?
Second, does my colleague believe that this is the type of board that, as the Bill suggests, should be located in Ottawa close to the Department of Transport, or could the independence of the commission be guaranteed by locating it elsewhere in the country away from the Department so that Canadians are assured that an independent group is carefully looking at what the cause of the accidents might be?
Third, in the Bill it states that public inquiries are an option. It seems to me that one of the big changes that we have tried to insist upon in the Government, both in environmental matters and in other matters, is that as a matter of fact public inquiries be considered as a way of proceeding. The fact that these are optional under the Bill surprises me. Does my colleague have any comments on that?

April 18, 1989
Transportation Accident Investigation Act

I agree with my colleague. I was concerned when I read the section in the Bill that only called for five members to be appointed by the Governor in Council. I was more concerned on the qualifications of the members. This was the point I raised earlier. I have now found the clause in the Bill which states:
4.(2) The Governor in Council shall appoint as members persons who, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, are collectively knowledgeable about air, marine, rail and commodity pipeline transportation.
I do not know where five members will be found to do that. It might have been better for the Government to get a few more experts in certain areas and increase the numbers on the Board.
As the Hon. Member mentioned, perhaps there is concern in other parts of the country that the Board may not be as independent if it is located close to Ottawa and the Department of Transport. In fact, Winnipeg might be a very good location for the Board.
We on this side are very concerned about the independence of the Board and the make-up of the members. Anything that will help to alleviate the concern in the public that the board is not independent will be a good step forward.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
It is interesting listening to the debate between Members of the Opposition Parties. Members of those Parties are giving out erroneous information to the Canadian public. Certain things must be recognized. Last year Pearson Airport had a 10 per cent increase in traffic, and the incidents that occurred at Pearson are actually down approximately 40 per cent. Are Members opposite listening? There has been a 10 per cent increase in traffic, but the incidents are down. Members opposite are attempting to tell everybody that everything is very unsafe. I notice that they still fly and come through Pearson on their way to Ottawa.
What we are talking about in the Bill is an investigation board that, when accidents occur or incidents occur, has the power to command that the Department people involved conduct the investigation, send them back to do things, make sure that the regulations in place are being followed, and if improvements can be made, then to make those type of adjustments.
That was not clearly spelled out in the CASB Act. The Bill now makes it clear that the Board must not hesitate to define and report fully on the cause of an accident, even when a person may incidentally be blamed thereby. This brings it out into the forefront and also gives the Board that power. When recommendations have been put forward and a Minister is not willing to follow those recommendations, he must give written reasons as to why he has not followed those recommendations.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to speak to this Bill. As Members who were here in the last Parliament, and indeed in two Parliaments before that will know, transportation safety has been an ongoing interest of mine, particularly when it comes to rail. I hope that the comments that I have to make today will be useful in terms of debating the whole matter of transportation safety in all modes.
I thought that the response just given by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Belsher)) was offered in a somewhat facetious manner. He pointed out the fact that Members of the Opposition still continue to fly through Toronto is some sort of proof of the insincerity of their criticism. This is really a threadbare argument. The fact is that many people in this country have to fly through Toronto if they want to do their job, if they want to continue living up to their responsibilities, whatever those responsibilities might be, whether they are in the business sector or politics, or whatever the case may be. For the Minister to suggest that because people have not reached the point of refusing to fly through Toronto there is not a problem, I think, with all due respect to the Parliamentary Secretary, is a particularly ignorant form of argument. I hope it is not repeated in future.
I fly from Ottawa to Winnipeg on a direct flight and I am very glad that I do not have to fly through Toronto, not just in terms of safety, but also in terms of delays, and planes being backed up for landing and backed up for taking off. If Tory Members who have to fly in and out of Toronto think that that is just great, that that is something they are willing to put up with in order to preserve the sacred ideological call of deregulation, then that is fine. Suffer, baby. The rest of us and the rest of Canadians ought not to suffer because of the ideological fixations of a Conservative Government.
April 18, 1989

The root of this matter is ideological. The root of everything that we are concerned about here today is the whole question of deregulation, a fixation, a trend which goes back to the Liberal Government of 1980 to 1984. I see the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Walker) starting to look a little uncomfortable. He knows that it was his political mentor, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), who started this trend toward deregulation. It was the Liberals who were first fascinated. They were saying: "What is going on? What are the Americans doing? We should do that too." The Liberals were as prone to that sort of thing as the Tories.
The Tories have finished the Liberal agenda on deregulation. They have completed what the Liberals started. We have a transportation system which is now fraught with confusion and danger. This Bill is designed as a kind of remedial action to pick up the pieces, to figure out what went wrong as a result of deregulation, not to address the root cause, not to address the fundamental problem of deregulation in and of itself, but simply to expedite the investigation of accidents that occur as a result of the kind of transportation system that the Conservatives have created through deregulation.
It is not going to work. It is not going to work because the fundamental problem of deregulation is not being addressed. The fundamental problem of putting airlines, railways, trucking companies, bus companies, and everyone else involved in the business of transportation in a position where they are in a kind of cut-throat relationship with each other, within modes and between modes, is going to create problems. I see it most clearly in the rail sector where the CPR and the CNR have been put in a position where they have to ruthlessly compete with each other. That means cutting comers, laying people off, not making investments that need to be made, not doing inspections that should be made, not doing maintenance that should be done.
They are competing with each other. As a group they are competing with the trucking companies which have also been put in a position where they are competing with each other. Almost anybody can get on the road if they have a couple of wheels to rub together. What have you got? You have a decrease in safety on the highways as a result of the new regulations with respect to trucking. You have problems in the rail sector. At a moment when the Government is doing a lot of talking about the Brundtland Commission, the environment and
Transportation Accident Investigation Act
everything else, we are in a deregulated policy framework that encourages trucking as opposed to rail. We know, and no one has ever disputed this, that rail traffic is an environmentally more suitable form of transportation than trucking.
This is one of the things that needs to be said in this debate, that to have this debate without debating deregulation is woefully inadequate. One of the things that bothers me about the Board, and it is a problem in many areas of Canadian life, is that boards accumulate political appointments. There is no guarantee that this Board will be any different.
I was reminded of that just a couple of weeks ago when I appeared before the National Transportation Agency. That is the Conservative substitute for the CTC, which in my judgment was not independent enough of the Government. It was an independent body, a quasi-judicial body which was replaced by the National Transportation Agency, which is much closer to the Government. That closeness could not be better demonstrated than by the fact that the chairman is a former Government House Leader for the Conservative Party, and an author of a report that at one time recommended severe cut-backs in VIA Rail.
It is a problem for many boards in Canada that they do accumulate political appointments. What happens is that people get appointed to these areas, but they do not necessarily know anything about them. They become dependant on the bureaucrats and the special advisers. Then the Government has special access, if I understand this legislation correctly, to draft reports. If there is something there that the Government does not like, it will have an opportunity to change it, or at least to try and change it.
These are some of the problems that we see with this legislation. It does not go to the heart of the matter. It does not solve the problems that were identified with the old board that this is replacing with respect to aviation safety. It does not address the whole question of deregulation. One of the things that I am particularly upset about in the last little while has been the decision of the courts to overturn the Larson report on the caboose decision. We see that the railways took the report of Mr. Larson, the arbitrator, after the railway strike, to court. The court overturned the report, which got in the way of the railway's plans to get rid of the caboose. This is very unfortunate. It is an example of the kind of thing that we have seen over the last few years.

April 18, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I rise to again draw the attention of the House to the tragic situation in Lebanon.
On Sunday, I attended a rally of some 500 persons in Halifax, organized by the Canadian Lebanon Society. I spoke with people whose relatives are living in shelters, and whose lives are imperilled on a daily basis.
Lebanese Canadians are convinced that Lebanese of all factions and religions can work together to work out their problems, if only the foreign interventionists can be removed.
I join with Lebanese Canadians of Nova Scotia in urging the Government of Canada to use its best influence and its position on the Security Council to introduce into the United Nations, or to inaugurate whatever measures are necessary to bring about the removal of all foreign forces from Lebanon, and an end to the slaughter of innocent people.
At the same time I would urge the Government of Canada to consider re-establishing effective consular services in Lebanon for the benefit of Canadians wishing to travel to and from that troubled land.

Mr. Speaker, later today the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) is to meet with representatives of native students, some of whom had been on a hunger strike for over three weeks. subtopic: LEBANON-CALL FOR SPECIAL MEETING OF UN SECURITY COUNCIL
LEBANON-CALL FOR SPECIAL MEETING OF UN SECURITY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the senseless killing of children and innocent adults and the destruction of property and essential services in Lebanon is a sad commentary, to say the least, on human history. In the last 41 days it is estimated that 262 people have been killed and 932 wounded.
Now is the time to find out if there is a will and a sincere desire on the part of other world nations to try to bring an end to the 14 years of bloodshed and civil war.
Any member of the UN Security Council has the right to ask for a special session of the Security Council to discuss an important issue. It does not have to come from the beleaguered country.
Therefore we call upon the Government of Canada to request a special meeting of the United Nations Security Council immediately to debate the issue of war-tom Lebanon with the aim of giving the UN Secretary General direction and support to undertake negotiations for meaningful peace.

Mr. Speaker, as this is National Citizenship Week it is a most appropriate time to reflect upon the many advantages our citizenship grants us.
Our citizenship is the envy of the world. It offers people a chance for social and personal advancement, and has given them scope for their talents and energies. All Canadians are guaranteed equality of access and opportunity.
In Canada, there are no degrees or levels of citizenship. We are all blessed with the right to freedom of thought, religious belief and self-expression. We are free to think what we want and to make active representations of those views within the political structure.

April 18, 1989
Another distinctive feature of our citizenship is its affirmation of the cultural heritage of all Canadian citizens.
Multiculturalism and the cross-cultural understanding that it engenders are now proudly recognized as fundamental components of our national identity and add much to our sense of being Canadian.
Citizenship Week is an ideal time to think about our Canadian identity and of how our civic values further this nation's evolution as a compassionate and caring society.
Let us use this week to celebrate our glorious birthright and to share our pride and our hope for the future.

subtopic: OPENING OF COAL MINE IN PICTOU COUNTY, NOVA SCOTIA-IMPACT ON CAPE BRETON
OPENING OF COAL MINE IN PICTOU COUNTY, NOVA SCOTIA-IMPACT ON CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent announcement by Westray Incorporated of their intention to open a new coal mine in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, with the assistance of the Government of Canada and the Government of Nova Scotia is frightening news for the employees of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. One of the founding principles of the Cape Breton Development Corporation was that it was to be the sole supplier of coal to the Government of Nova Scotia's wholly-owned Nova Scotia Power Corporation. Now that the federal and provincial Governments have broken this undertaking, much economic hardship will occur to the people of Cape Breton.
Why, Mr. Speaker, is the Government of Canada and the Government of Nova Scotia putting one poor area of a small province against another poor area of the same province? Should this particular operation proceed, it is inevitable, Mr. Speaker, that a coal mine in Cape Breton will be closed, throwing countless miners out of work. It will substantially reduce the revenue for the Cape Breton Development Corporation. It will also reduce a market for their particular product. I urge, Mr. Speaker, that the Government of Canada and the Government of Nova Scotia withdraw their proposed financial assistance to this particular operation and stop playing the cheapest political game in town which is setting one poor area off against another poor area.
April 18, 1989

subtopic: FUNDING FOR RECONSTRUCTION OF TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY IN NEW BRUNSWICK
FUNDING FOR RECONSTRUCTION OF TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY IN NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that all Hon. Members await the Finance Minister's Budget next week with both a sense of concern and resolve. We all know that priority choices will be difficult to make. Many essential decisions will be even more difficult to take. I want to mention one such priority briefly, Mr. Speaker, which is of great concern to New Brunswickers. That is the pressing and serious need for reconstruction of our Trans-Canada Highway from the Quebec border to the Nova Scotia border which is indisputably the worst highway in the country. While I realize that highways are essentially a provincial responsibility, it is obvious that in the long run, with the total cost of the Trans-Canada Highway itself, not including connectors, estimated in the range of $15 billion in 1988, it would be impossible to conceive such a major undertaking without the federal Government's participation.
I would suggest it is important for us to recognize such a priority even though it may presently be impossible to determine the timing or the terms of such a commitment. What is clear and compelling is the fact that New Brunswick's Trans-Canada Highway is virtually obsolete, totally inadequate and truly dangerous. The time will come and soon when New Brunswick and Canada will have no alternative but to find a way to rebuild it completely. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: MEAT INSPECTION PRACTICES AT THE BORDER
MEAT INSPECTION PRACTICES AT THE BORDER
speechtext:
The Government is showing a cavalier disregard for the health of Canadians in the confusion it is allowing to continue around meat inspection practices at the border into Canada. The net effect has been for taxes on the rich to go down by over 6 per cent while taxes on middle-income people went up 17 per cent and personal taxes for the working poor in Canada went up by a whopping 60 per cent.
Since he has always talked about fairness before Budgets, is this what fairness has meant for the Conservatives, and is this what the working poor and average Canadians will see in the coming Budget?

Mr. Speaker, I have not had occasion to look at the document to which my hon. friend refers, but in general terms he seems to be talking about the working poor and greater social justice. He would probably agree that over the last four years the creation of 1.4 million new jobs is the greatest contribution to social justice that a Government could make.
The number of Canadians living below the poverty line has fallen by 549,000 since 1984, including 179,000 fewer children and 61,000 fewer senior citizens. I know my hon. friend would agree that those are very important social policy considerations.
I think we have made much progress toward a greater degree of social justice. We can surely do a lot more, and hopefully the Budget and the actions of this Parliament over the next four years will improve upon an already enviable record.

The only reason I interrupt the Hon. Member is so that we can have a little more quiet in the House. I think that would
